The word "offertory" belongs to the world of Christian religious services. It has three closely related meanings — all rooted in a single idea: the act of offering something to God. Once you understand that core idea, the whole word makes sense.
1. A named section of a church service

Many Christian churches — particularly Catholic, Anglican (Church of England), Lutheran, and other churches that follow a fixed, structured order of worship — divide their services into named parts that follow the same sequence every week. The offertory is one of these parts.

It falls roughly in the middle of the service: after the scripture readings and the sermon, but before the central prayer (in a Catholic Mass, that's the Eucharistic Prayer, which leads up to Communion).

What happens during the offertory? A few things, all of which involve presenting or offering something:

  • In Catholic and Anglican churches, members of the congregation carry bread and wine to the altar (the central table at the front of the church). The priest then says specific prayers to formally present these gifts to God. This is the heart of the offertory — a solemn act of offering.
  • In most churches, the congregation offers their own personal gift in the form of money, which brings us to the second meaning.

Also during the offertory, plates, baskets, or bags are passed through the pews, and people place money, cheques, or giving envelopes into them as their personal contribution to the church and as an act of giving to God.

This is the meaning most people recognise from attending church. When someone says "the offertory was very generous this Sunday," they almost certainly mean the money collected from the congregation at that point in the service.

So "offertory" can refer to:

  • The act of collecting from the congregation, or
  • The money itself that was collected.

Both usages are correct and common.
3. The music performed during this time

The offertory portion of a service takes several minutes — plates need to be passed, bread and wine need to be brought forward, the altar needs to be prepared. To fill this time reverently, music is sung or played. This music is also called the offertory — or more specifically, an offertory anthem, offertory hymn, or offertory motet.

In the ancient Latin Catholic Mass, there was a specific chant assigned to each Sunday and feast day of the year (with words drawn mostly from the Book of Psalms), sung precisely at this point in the service. It was called the Offertory antiphon.

As Western music developed over the centuries, composers began writing elaborate choral pieces and orchestral works to be performed here. These are called "offertories" or "offertory motets," and composers as famous as Mozart, Handel, and Schubert wrote them. When a church musician says "we'll be singing an offertory by Mozart," they mean a choral composition intended specifically to be performed during the offertory section of a Mass.

They are not really three separate meanings — they are three faces of the same moment in a service. The offertory is the time of offering, and it gave its name naturally to:

  • The musical piece played during that time,
  • The collection of gifts that takes place during that time,
  • And the whole moment itself in the order of service.

Context always tells you which face of the word is being used. In a sentence about a church service's structure, it means the liturgical moment. In a sentence about money raised, it means the collection. In a sentence about a composer or a choir, it means a piece of music.

Even in Protestant churches that don't follow a strict, formally named order of service (such as many Baptist or Evangelical congregations), the word "offertory" is sometimes used informally to mean the time when the collection is taken and the music played during that time — even if the church doesn't officially call it by that name.
Example sentences to sharpen your understanding

• "After the sermon, the congregation rose for the offertory hymn while the ushers passed the baskets." → offertory as music
  • "During the offertory, two parishioners carried the bread and wine to the altar." → offertory as the liturgical moment
  • "The offertory this Christmas Eve was the largest the parish had received in a decade." → offertory as the money collected
  • "The choir performed a magnificent offertory by Handel before the Eucharistic Prayer began." → offertory as a composed musical work
  • "Please remain seated during the offertory." → offertory as a section of the service

If you ever forget the details, remember this: offertory = the moment of offering in a church service. Everything else — the music, the collection, the ritual presentation of bread and wine — flows from that single act of giving something to God. The word is simply the name for that moment and everything belonging to it.
